The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighErrorRate on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T02:05:23Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T02:05:48Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
Broken from 2026-11-11T01:58:00Z {began} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute) to 2026-11-11T02:11:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 13 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 6 minutes 28 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T02:12:13Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.0% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 29.5% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 37.5% {errors_at_worst}.
Rise above baseline: 28.5% {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The series behind the alert, `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))` - its alert said "Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 0.975% {series_before} before it began, 29.46153846153846% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 37.5% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
Customer loss: 8,241.24 USD {customer_loss} - how far the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier, beyond how much those hours vary on their own.

  - [T26] 2026-11-11T02:10:43Z {T26.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 02:11 {T26.2} - up to 144s {T26.3}
  - [T27] 2026-11-11T02:12:13Z {T27.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 02:11 {T27.2}

  - [T30] 2026-11-11T02:13:42Z {T30.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/525
A person's message never stops a step already running: between steps, Argus starts no new one while a message waits to be answered.

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-11-11T01:58:33Z {P1.1} flag-toggle legacy-checkout-fallback by admin: feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off
  - [P2] 2026-11-11T01:58:33Z {P2.1} flag-toggle monthly-spend-feature by admin: feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on
  - Deploys read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [G153f] INFO io-shop: legacy-checkout-fallback=on - 200 {G153f.1} evaluations - 30 {G153f.2} occurrences in 30 {G153f.3} minutes, 01:28–01:57 {G153f.4}
  - [G7e5d] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off - 200 {G7e5d.1} evaluations - 30 {G7e5d.2} occurrences in 30 {G7e5d.3} minutes, 01:28–01:57 {G7e5d.4}
  - [Gc27d] INFO io-shop: account pages served - # by the legacy renderer, # by the new renderer - 38 {Gc27d.1} occurrences in 38 {Gc27d.2} minutes, 01:28–02:05 {Gc27d.3}; # was 0 {Gc27d.4} to 200 {Gc27d.5}, typically 200 {Gc27d.6}, highest at 01:28 {Gc27d.7}; # was 0 {Gc27d.8} to 200 {Gc27d.9}, typically 0 {Gc27d.10}, highest at 01:59 {Gc27d.11}
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 41 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 30 {G46bc.2} minutes, 01:28–01:57 {G46bc.3}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 32 {Gbac1.1} occurrences in 38 {Gbac1.2} minutes, 01:28–02:05 {Gbac1.3}; # was 0.50% {Gbac1.4} to 35.00% {Gbac1.5}, typically 1.50% {Gbac1.6}, highest at 02:02 {Gbac1.7}
  - [Gad41] INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 6 {Gad41.1} occurrences in 27 {Gad41.2} minutes, 01:29–01:55 {Gad41.3}
  - [G7ad6] INFO io-shop: legacy-checkout-fallback=off 83 {G7ad6.1} / on 117 {G7ad6.2} - 200 {G7ad6.3} evaluations - 1 {G7ad6.4} occurrence in 1 {G7ad6.5} minute, 01:58 {G7ad6.6}
  - [G971b] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off 113 {G971b.1} / on 87 {G971b.2} - 200 {G971b.3} evaluations - 1 {G971b.4} occurrence in 1 {G971b.5} minute, 01:58 {G971b.6}
  - [G5309] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ZeroDivisionError: division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 - 16 {G5309.1} occurrences in 8 {G5309.2} minutes, 01:58–02:05 {G5309.3}
  - [G7037] INFO io-shop: legacy-checkout-fallback=off - 200 {G7037.1} evaluations - 7 {G7037.2} occurrences in 7 {G7037.3} minutes, 01:59–02:05 {G7037.4}
  - [Gce95] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=on - 200 {Gce95.1} evaluations - 7 {Gce95.2} occurrences in 7 {Gce95.3} minutes, 01:59–02:05 {Gce95.4}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] At 2026-11-11T01:58:33Z {C1.1} the feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on. Account page requests then began failing with ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, taking the error rate from about 1% {C1.2} to about 34% {C1.3}. No deployment was involved, the rollout converged, and latency and resources stayed flat. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.55 {C1.4}, refuted]
  - [C2] At 2026-11-11T01:58:33Z {C2.1} the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off. Account pages moved from the legacy renderer to the new renderer, which raises the ZeroDivisionError. The new-renderer count at 01:58 {C2.2} (83 {C2.3}) equals the flag's off-evaluation count (83 {C2.4}). [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.38 {C2.5}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature for [C1] (can be put back) - refuted, put back when it did not help
  - [M2] Reverted the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback for [C2] (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault: `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py ends with `account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)` (line 47 {F1.1}, the line the ZeroDivisionError names). `bought_this_month` holds only the purchases flagged `in_current_month`, so for any shopper who has bought before but not this month the list is empty and the division raises. The tests already describe that shopper as the ordinary case. Any account page that reaches this figure fails at the request boundary in src/io_shop/account_page.py, which records the error and returns a failed page. Turning the flag off stopped traffic reaching this path but did not fix the arithmetic, so turning it back on would bring the failures straight back.
      
      The change: when nothing was bought this month, the function returns 0 {F1.2}. That is the true figure: the shopper has spent nothing per item this month. Otherwise the calculation is unchanged. The lifetime average, `render_spend_summary` and the boundary's broad catch are untouched. The existing test that the lifetime path still raises for an account with no purchases at all still holds, so failures elsewhere are not hidden.
      
      The test: tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py gains cases that call `average_spend_per_item_this_month` directly, and `render_spend_summary(..., use_monthly_summary=True)`, on an account with past purchases but none this month. Both expect 0 {F1.3}. Against the current code both calls raise ZeroDivisionError.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Reverted the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #525 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P1].

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

What people working the incident wrote in its thread:
  - L1 (Some Person, 2026-11-11T02:06:31Z): "it's legacy-checkout-fallback - someone switched it off right before this started" - the investigation found it unverified: legacy-checkout-fallback did switch off at 2026-11-11T01:58:33Z, but monthly-spend-feature was switched on at the same instant, and the ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py:47 points at the spend feature, so the evidence can't isolate the fallback flag.
Each was weighed on what the investigation had read, before anything was tried. Where the actions above say otherwise, the actions are the later word.
For each, say in lead_effects whether it changed what was done.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: Switching legacy-checkout-fallback off sent account pages to the new renderer, and those pages reach average_spend_per_item_this_month in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. Code-Fix read that function as dividing this month's spend total by the number of purchases made this month, with nothing to handle a month with no purchases. So for any shopper who has bought before but not this month, the division raises ZeroDivisionError and the account page fails. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
cause_in_plain_words: Someone turned off a setting that kept account pages on their older version, which sent shoppers to a newer version that likely breaks when it works out an average of this month's spending for anyone who has bought nothing this month.
still_at_risk: If legacy-checkout-fallback is switched off again, the new renderer would serve account pages again, and they would fail for shoppers who have bought nothing this month.
symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
lead_effects L1: It did not change what was done: the lead was weighed as unverified, monthly-spend-feature was reverted first, and the flag it named was turned back on only after that revert was refuted, as the Investigator's second candidate.
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' account pages failed: account page requests came back as failed pages, and the logged account-page error rate peaked at {Gbac1.7}. (cites G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2: Account page requests raised a ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1} of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py over {G5309.3}, and each request that raised it failed. (cites G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 3: At {P1.1} the flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off, and account pages moved from the legacy renderer to the new one. At {G7ad6.6}, {G7ad6.1} of the flag's evaluations read off. Over {G7037.4} every evaluation read off. The new renderer's count of account pages served was highest at {Gc27d.11}, after being typically {Gc27d.10} before. (cites P1, under "Changes to production it read"; G7ad6, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G7037, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gc27d, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 3 ruled_out 1: The switch-on of monthly-spend-feature at {P2.1}, made at the same instant (candidate C1). Turning that flag back off left the service at the incident's level, so the flag was put back on. (cites T19, under "What Argus did, in order"; T21, under "What Argus did, in order"; T22, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 4: Pages served by the new renderer reach average_spend_per_item_this_month, which, as Code-Fix reads it, divides by the number of purchases made this month and so fails for any shopper who has bought nothing this month. (cites F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix"; G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gc27d, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
contributing_factors 1: Before legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off in production, no check was seen that the new renderer serves an account with past purchases but none this month.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: Such a check would likely have failed before the flag was switched, and shoppers would never have reached the failing path.
contributing_factors 2: The flag change moved all account-page traffic to the new renderer at once. Every evaluation read off from the minute after the switch, and no staged rollout or automatic halt on rising errors was seen.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: A staged switch with a halt on rising errors would have limited the failures to a small share of shoppers and turned the flag back sooner.
contributing_factors 3: legacy-checkout-fallback and monthly-spend-feature were changed by the same admin at the same instant, and the error named the spend-summary code. That made it hard to tell which change caused the failures.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: With the changes made apart, the onset would have pointed at the fallback flag alone, and the first revert would have been the one that worked, so the incident would have been shorter.
action_items 1: Before a flag is switched in production, require a test run of the code path it turns on. For legacy-checkout-fallback, that means the new renderer serving an account with past purchases but none this month.
action_items 2: Roll out flag changes that move account pages between renderers in stages, with an automatic halt and revert when the account-page error rate rises.
action_items 3: Make production flag changes on io-shop one at a time, with enough time between them to tell their effects apart.
action_items 4: Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.
went_wrong 1: Nobody was paged. No on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was called in to work it.
went_wrong 2: The investigation ranked monthly-spend-feature above legacy-checkout-fallback because the error named the spend-summary code, so the first revert went to the wrong flag. Yet the new renderer's count at the onset matched the fallback flag's off evaluations, and the thread had named the fallback flag.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
